To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cocaine administration to juvenile mice induces a rapid and long-lasting increase in the number of synapses onto dopamine neurons, and that this effect is associated with the reappearance, in a subset of synapses, of AMPARs lacking the GluA2 subunit and of NMDARs containing the GluN1 and GluN3 subunits.
the expression of the GluA2 and GluN1 subunits of AMPARs and NR1 subunits of NMDARs are developmentally regulated.
cocaine triggers glutamate receptor changes that resemble those that occur during the postnatal critical period of synaptic development.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms of synaptic plasticity and their role in learning and memory, and with the role of synaptic plasticity in the development of addiction.
the mechanisms underlying the development of synaptic function in the VTA and the effects of addictive drugs on these developmental processes.
the molecular mechanisms that underlie the maturation of glutamatergice synapses onto dopamine neurons in the ventro-tegmental area (VTA), the major site for the initiation of drug addiction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data are not conclusive.
addictive drugs trigger a drug-evoked plasticity in which the immature synapse is re-established, but it is unclear if this is the same process as the developmental critical period.
drug-evoked synaptic plasticity is an intriguing hypothesis, which has been supported by some experimental evidence but is still in need of further investigation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the drug-evoked plasticity of glutamate receptors at the synapse onto VTA DA neurons is a key factor for the development of addiction to cocaine.
addictive drugs may reopen the critical period of glutamatergice receptor maturation and that the resulting synaptic changes are important for the rewarding effects of the drugs.
cocaine-induced plasticity in the VTA is mediated by the activation of the NMDA receptor.
The main takeaway from our work is that

drug-evoked plasticity is a general phenomenon that occurs in many parts of the CNS and that the developmental critical period hypothesis is a good model to explain how drugs of abuse can induce lasting synaptic and circuit changes.
the developmental critical period is not a fixed period of time, but rather a dynamic state that is influenced by experience and can be reopened by drugs of abuse.
addictive drugs can trigger the re-expression of immature synaptic phenotypes, and these phenotypes are associated with increased synaptic plasticity and enhanced vulnerability to addiction.
